# Watching the Light

A drawing is a choice about what to notice. In this booklet we will notice one thing: where a patch of sunlight falls on the classroom floor.

## What we will do

The activity takes place over three school days. You will work with the same partner each day. You will make an observation at the beginning of the morning lesson and another immediately after lunch. That gives six observations in all.

We do this more than once because one drawing cannot show whether a position changes. It shows only where the light was, once. Several drawings can show more.

Our drawings will show where the light can be seen. They will not tell us why it is there. That is a different question, and the drawings do not answer it.

## How to mark the floor plan

Mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan. Write the time beside it.

Sometimes the edge of the light is fuzzy. Where it is, draw that part with a dotted line. Do not decide that the edge must be sharp just because a sharp line is easier to draw. A pencil and ruler are provided, but the ruler does not make a fuzzy edge less fuzzy. It is good for straight lines. It cannot tell you where the light ends.

You may find that another group has marked the edge differently. Do not change your drawing straight away, and do not tell them to change theirs. First compare what each of you noticed. Then decide whether either drawing needs to change.

## When there is no light

Some days the patch may not be visible. When that happens, write "no patch visible" in the space for that observation. Leave the map unmarked. Do not draw where the patch was yesterday. That would be a map of yesterday.

"No patch visible" counts as an observation. It does not count as a measurement of the patch's position, because there was no position to measure.

The curtains will stay in their usual position. We will not control the clouds, and we will not record how thick they are. So we will not know why a patch is missing. We will know only that we did not see it.

## At the end

Compare all six observation spaces with your partner. Then write:

- one sentence about a pattern you can support
- one question that remains

Perhaps too few patches were visible to show a pattern. If so, say that, and explain which observations are missing.

You are not required to discover a particular pattern. A careful account of what could not be observed can be more useful than a confident account of a patch nobody saw.

# New in this release: Pause on Focus

This release adds **Pause on Focus**, an option for people who use a keyboard to navigate and listen to spoken image descriptions. You'll find it in the **Reading** settings.

## What it does

By default, nothing changes. If an image description has started speaking and you move keyboard focus to another control, the description keeps going. Pause on Focus gives you the alternative.

With the option **turned on**:

- Moving keyboard focus to a different control pauses the image description that is speaking.
- Returning focus to the image does **not** resume it automatically.
- To hear the description again, use the existing **Read Description** command. It plays from the beginning.

"Pause" here means the speech stops and the saved description is kept. It does not mean playback picks up at the word where it stopped. The descriptions themselves are not changed.

## How it fits with your other settings

- **Automatic image descriptions:** If you previously turned these off, they stay off after updating. Pause on Focus does not turn them on.
- **Manually requested descriptions:** The option also pauses these, so it is useful even with automatic descriptions disabled.

## What it does not cover

Pause on Focus only affects descriptions spoken by this application. It will not necessarily stop all speech when focus moves:

- **Separate screen readers:** Speech from a screen reader is controlled by that screen reader, even when it is describing the same image.
- **Video audio:** Sound inside a video is controlled by the video player.

If two sources of speech are active at once, these limits may explain why you still hear something after focus moves.

## Availability

Pause on Focus is available in the **desktop application only**. The mobile version keeps its existing behavior.

## Reporting a problem

If a description keeps speaking after focus has visibly moved, please let us know. If you can tell whether the speech came from the application or from a separate screen reader, include that, but you don't need to work it out before reporting. It helps most if you tell us which action moved focus. Please don't send the contents of the image.

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might reduce the time water remained above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed during four storms before and four storms after a cover change. The three drains on the lower street received new covers; the three on the upper street retained their existing covers. Allocation was not random: crews selected the lower street because it had received more complaints.

Fixed cameras recorded the minutes water remained above a painted reference line at each drain during each storm. All 48 drain-storm observations were available. A recorded duration of zero indicates no visible water above the line, not an absence of runoff. Across the twelve observations for each street in each period, mean duration fell from 18 to 10 minutes on the lower street and from 9 to 7 minutes on the upper street. The lower street therefore showed an eight-minute reduction, compared with a two-minute reduction on the upper street. This larger reduction can inform further study, but the comparison does not by itself establish an effect of the new covers.

Several factors limit interpretation. The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier storms. Neither street had a local gauge, and within-storm rainfall intensity was not measured. Crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because the initial quantity of leaves was not recorded, cleaning cannot be assumed to explain the larger improvement on the lower street. Equally, cleaning cannot be dismissed as irrelevant simply because both streets received it. These uncertainties, together with the nonrandom allocation of covers, leave the contribution of the cover change unresolved.

The camera records establish shorter durations above the reference line at both sets of drains during the later period. They do not establish increased drainage capacity, which was not directly measured, or fewer flooded properties, which was not measured at all. The pilot included no property-damage observations. Peak water depth could also change in a way that matters even if duration remained unchanged, but peak depth was not extracted from the images.

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and debris quantities before cleaning. These measures would address some of the present ambiguities, although rotation alone would not make storms identical. The existing recordings remain useful for describing conditions during these eight storms and assessing the practicality of the camera-based duration measure. Staff reported that every recording could be scored; whether different scorers assign the same duration remains untested.

## What was measured

The pilot asked whether a different grate cover might shorten the time water stayed above the pavement after rain. We observed six drains on two streets during eight storms: four before a cover change and four after. The three drains on the lower street received the new covers. The three on the upper street kept their original covers. Cover allocation was not random. The lower street was chosen because crews had received more complaints there.

| Street | Cover change | Mean minutes above line, before (12 observations) | Mean minutes above line, after (12 observations) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lower | New covers | 18 | 10 | −8 |
| Upper | Original covers | 9 | 7 | −2 |

Recorded durations were shorter at both sets of drains in the later period, and the reduction was larger on the lower street. This is a description of the recordings. It may help in deciding what to study next, but it does not by itself identify an effect of the cover.

## What the measurements cannot explain

Several factors changed or varied alongside the covers, and the pilot cannot separate them:

- **Non-random allocation.** The lower street was selected because it had more complaints, and it also started with longer durations (18 minutes against 9). The two streets may differ in ways that affect both ponding and how they change over time, so the comparison between them is not a like-for-like test.
- **Rainfall.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier four. Neither street had its own gauge, and the pilot has no within-storm intensity measurements. Lighter rain alone could produce shorter durations at both sets of drains, and we cannot say how much of the change it accounts for.
- **Simultaneous cleaning.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. The initial quantity of leaves was not recorded. We therefore cannot say that cleaning explains why the lower street improved more, and we cannot rule it out. Cleaning both streets does not make it irrelevant, because the lower street may have had more debris to remove.

## What was not measured

The camera records show shorter durations above the line. They should not be read as evidence of the following:

- **Drainage capacity.** It was not directly measured, so an increase in capacity is not established.
- **Flooded properties.** The pilot made no property-damage observations, and fewer flooded properties is not something these data can show.
- **Peak water depth.** A change in peak depth could matter even if duration did not change, but depth was not extracted from the images.

## Reliability of the duration measure

Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. We have not tested whether different scorers assign the same duration to the same recording, so the consistency of the measure is unknown.

## Possible follow-up design

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and the amount of debris before cleaning. That would address some of the ambiguities above, though rotation alone would not make storms identical. Separately, a scorer-agreement check would show whether the camera-based duration measure is dependable.

## What the existing recordings can support

The recordings remain useful for describing these eight storms and for assessing whether camera-based duration is a practical measure. They do not establish that the new covers shortened ponding.

# Does Diagram Placement Affect Pupils' Explanations of Water Level?

*A materials evaluation report*

## What we compared

We prepared two versions of a worksheet that asked pupils to explain why the same amount of water looks different in a tall vessel and a wide vessel.

- **Version A (side-by-side):** a diagram appeared beside each question.
- **Version B (reference page):** the same diagrams were grouped together on a separate reference page.

The wording, diagrams, and order of questions were otherwise identical.

## How the materials were used

Four classes used the worksheets during one lesson. Two classes received A and two received B. Teachers chose the version for their classes before seeing any pupil responses. Classes were not assigned at random.

Teachers used the same written instructions, but they were free to answer pupils' questions during the lesson. We did not record those exchanges.

## Who is included

The analysis covers returned worksheets only: 52 for Version A and 49 for Version B. Six pupils assigned A and five assigned B were absent and are not counted.

## How answers were scored

A scorer who could not see the worksheet layout assessed transcribed answers to the final explanation question. Each answer could earn up to two points:

- one point for stating that the amount of water was unchanged
- one point for explaining that vessel shape changed the water level

## Results

| Score | Version A (n = 52) | Version B (n = 49) |
|---|---|---|
| Both points | 31 | 27 |
| One point | 15 | 16 |
| Zero | 6 | 6 |

Fully credited answers made up about 60% of Version A worksheets (31 of 52) and about 55% of Version B worksheets (27 of 49). Zero-scoring answers were equally common in the two groups, at six each.

## Main finding

The side-by-side layout (A) was associated with a somewhat larger share of fully credited answers in these classes. The difference is small.

## Limitations

- **Class and teacher effects.** Pupils were not randomly assigned, and each version was used by only two classes. The evaluation cannot separate the effect of layout from differences between classes.
- **Unrecorded teacher help.** Teachers could answer questions, and we did not record what they said. Classroom assistance may have differed between versions, so the comparison cannot be treated as a controlled test of the worksheets alone.
- **Unknown starting knowledge.** We did not score an earlier baseline task, so we do not know whether the groups began with similar understanding.
- **One question only.** The scores come from a single question. They are response scores, not a measure of pupils' general understanding of volume.
- **Limited scoring check.** A second scorer re-scored ten transcribed answers and agreed with the first on nine. Discussion resolved the tenth before the final totals above were compiled. This describes the scoring procedure but is not a complete reliability study.
- **No preference data.** We asked no preference question, so the evaluation does not show which layout pupils preferred.

## What this evaluation provides

The work gives a concrete comparison of the returned answers from these four classes. It also shows what a more controlled evaluation would need to record: how pupils are assigned to versions, a baseline measure, the help teachers give during the lesson, and, if preference matters, a direct question about it.

# Briefing: Automatic Flood Warning Signs for the Underpass

## Recommendation

Install the proposed automatic warning signs, on condition that the same decision also:

1. names a team responsible for monthly sensor checks, and
2. provides a manual closure procedure for when the system is unavailable.

Staff time for these checks has not yet been allocated. Until it is, the purchase is not ready for approval. Leaving the condition implicit would be misleading.

## What the signs do and do not do

The underpass sometimes fills with water before a maintenance crew can close the road. The signs address that delay by warning drivers sooner. They will not keep water out. Installing them would complete a warning project, not the flood work, and the drainage problem would remain unresolved.

Because signs cannot prevent every unsafe entry, some drivers will still overlook or disregard them. That is not a reason to reject warning equipment. It is a reason to describe accurately what the equipment does.

## Cost and comparison with pipe replacement

- Installing two signs is estimated at 18,000 units of local currency.
- Replacing the drainage pipe is estimated at 140,000.
- Neither estimate includes annual maintenance.

The signs are a smaller initial purchase, but they are not a measured substitute for the pipe. We have no agreed estimate of how much either option would reduce injuries or vehicle damage. The signs should be judged as a response to delayed warnings, not as a cheaper way to achieve the same outcome as the pipe.

## Why the maintenance and closure conditions matter

The signs activate when a water-level sensor crosses a set threshold. The sensor can fail, and the signs need power. A dark sign therefore cannot safely be read as "the road is clear," since it may mean the system is unavailable.

The proposal includes a permanent notice telling drivers that water may be present even when the electronic sign is off. This helps, but it does not solve the problem of drivers missing or ignoring warnings. Monthly sensor checks reduce the chance that the system is silently down. The manual closure procedure covers the periods when it is.

## Relationship to the drainage project

Pipe replacement remains a separate option that requires design work. Buying signs should not be described as approving or rejecting it.

There is a reasonable concern that a visible new device will reduce pressure to fix the drainage itself. We can answer part of that concern by requiring the next infrastructure report to state the pipe project's status explicitly. A reporting requirement cannot guarantee construction, and this briefing does not claim that it can.

# Proposal: Report excluded runs in a separate table

**Status:** Proposed for discussion. Not yet adopted.

## The problem

The final summary currently lists only the runs used to calculate the reported mean. That makes the mean easy to read, but a reader cannot tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether the exclusions simply disappeared from the summary.

## Proposed policy

1. **Add an exclusions table to the report template.** It would be labeled as a record of exclusions and would list every excluded run. Each row would give:
   - run identifier
   - completion status
   - reason for exclusion
   - whether a usable reading exists

2. **Report counts beside the mean.** The summary would state the number of runs attempted and the number retained. The exclusions table would account for the difference.

3. **Allow a shared explanation for a group of runs.** When one fault affects several runs, the reason can be written once. Each affected run must still appear as its own row.

4. **Leave raw readings out of the table.** They would remain in the underlying record, available through the existing review process.

5. **Do not change the exclusion rule.** The table would only show how the existing rule was applied. It does not propose that every excluded reading enter the mean.

## Reasoning

**Why exclusions need a record.** The existing rule distinguishes two cases, and the table lets a reader see which one applied to each run.
- A run stopped by a temperature controller failure did not meet the stated measurement conditions, so it is excluded.
- A completed run with an unusual result is retained. An unusual result alone does not show that the conditions failed. It is excluded only if a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies it.

**Why the table lists runs rather than values.** A table of excluded numeric values would miss runs that produced no usable reading, which could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was. $$

# Orthogonal projection onto the permitted displacements

## Statement

Let P be a real d×d matrix with d ≥ 1 such that

- **(H1) idempotent:** P² = P
- **(H2) symmetric:** Pᵀ = P

Let S = {Pz : z ∈ ℝᵈ} be the set of permitted layout displacements, and write ‖v‖² = vᵀv.

**Claim.** For every x ∈ ℝᵈ and every y ∈ S,

‖x − y‖² = ‖x − Px‖² + ‖Px − y‖².

Consequently Px is the unique point of S that minimizes ‖x − y‖².

Here x is the requested displacement, Px is the nearest permitted displacement, and x − Px is the part of the request that is discarded.

## Proof

Fix x ∈ ℝᵈ and y ∈ S, and write y = Pz for some z.

**Step 1: P fixes every element of S (uses H1).**
Since P² = P, we have P(Px) = Px, and Py = P(Pz) = P²z = Pz = y. So P acts as the identity on S. In particular, Px ∈ S and y ∈ S, and by linearity

P(Px − y) = Px − y.  (1)

**Step 2: P removes the discarded part (uses H1).**
P(x − Px) = Px − P²x = Px − Px = 0.  (2)

**Step 3: The discarded part is orthogonal to S (uses H1 and H2).**
Let u = x − Px and w = Px − y. We show uᵀw = 0:

| | Reason |
|---|---|
| uᵀw = uᵀ(Pw) | By (1), Pw = w. |
| = (Pᵀu)ᵀw = (Pu)ᵀw | Moving P onto u is the one place symmetry (H2) is needed, since (uᵀP)ᵀ = Pᵀu = Pu. |
| = 0ᵀw = 0 | By (2), Pu = 0. |

Without H2, P could be a non-orthogonal projection, and u would not be perpendicular to w.

**Step 4: Expand the squared norm.**
Since x − y = u + w,

‖x − y‖² = ‖u‖² + 2uᵀw + ‖w‖².

The cross term is zero by Step 3, which gives the identity:

‖x − y‖² = ‖x − Px‖² + ‖Px − y‖².

**Step 5: Minimality and uniqueness.**
In the identity, the first term on the right does not depend on y, and the second is nonnegative. So for every y ∈ S, ‖x − y‖² ≥ ‖x − Px‖². Since Px ∈ S (Step 1), it attains this lower bound, so it is a minimizer.

If some y ∈ S also attains the minimum, so that ‖x − y‖² = ‖x − Px‖², the identity forces ‖Px − y‖² = 0. Hence y = Px, and the minimizer is unique. ∎

## Edge cases and scope

- **Zero-dimensional S.** If P = 0, then S = {0}. Steps 1–5 hold unchanged: y = 0, Px = 0, and the identity reads ‖x‖² = ‖x‖² + 0. The unique minimizer is 0. (The converse also holds: S = {0} only when P = 0.)
- **P = I.** Then S = ℝᵈ, Px = x, and the residual x − Px is zero. The identity reduces to ‖x − y‖² = ‖x − y‖².
- **No inverse or rank assumption.** Only H1 and H2 are used. For any P with 0 ≤ rank P ≤ d satisfying them, the argument works as written, and P is not assumed invertible. In fact, the only invertible P satisfying H1 is I.
- **Scope.** The result concerns squared Euclidean distance to this fixed subspace S. It says nothing about other layout constraints, such as inequality bounds or non-Euclidean costs.

$$

$$

Focus lock keeps keyboard focus inside the current dialog until the dialog closes. It is useful when controls behind the dialog remain visible but should not receive keyboard input. Focus lock does not freeze the pointer, and it does not prevent the user from closing the dialog with the documented close command.

The implementation uses a sentinel at each end of the dialog's tab sequence. When focus reaches a sentinel, the handler moves it to the appropriate control at the opposite end. This is a focus-management mechanism, not a security boundary. Code running in the page can still move focus deliberately, so the application must handle those changes rather than assume the lock prevents them.

To test focus lock, open the dialog, traverse its controls in both directions, and close it while focus is on the last control. Focus should return to the control that opened the dialog. If that control has been removed, the application uses its documented fallback target. The fallback is part of the application's behavior and is not chosen by focus lock itself.

A separate hardware example describes a switch whose spring contacts latch when pressed. That use of latch refers to the physical mechanism. The example does not demonstrate the software feature and should not be used as a test of it.

You will need the paper bridge, the tray, and the bag of counters from your group's box. Put the tray in the middle of the table and place the bridge across the tray. The bridge should rest on the two wooden blocks, not on the tray's rim. The tray is there to catch counters if they fall, so check that the tray sits under the middle of the bridge.

Before adding any counters, sketch the bridge from the side. Mark where the bridge touches the blocks. Then put one counter in the centre of the bridge and sketch the bridge again. Your second sketch should show the bridge, including any bend you can see, rather than just the new counter. If you cannot see a bend, say so beside the sketch.

Add counters one at a time, placing each on the same marked spot. After each addition, wait until the bridge stops moving before deciding whether to add another. The counters should stay in the tray if the bridge collapses. Do not rebuild the bridge during this first test, even if you have a promising idea about making it stronger.

When the test ends, count the counters that were on the bridge immediately before the bridge collapsed. If you stop because you have used all twelve counters and the bridge is still standing, record “held twelve; collapse not observed.” That is different from saying the bridge can hold exactly twelve.

Now discuss one change you would like to test next time. Keep your first sketches. Those sketches record what this bridge did before the change, which will be useful when your next bridge behaves differently from the one you imagined.

We are asking households in selected blocks to tell us about one day’s travel. Your household’s response is useful even if everyone stayed home. Households that make few or no trips are among those we want to hear from.

The enclosed card gives your household a date. Please describe that day, even if it was unusual for you. We are asking about a specific day from everyday life, rather than a day you choose as typical.

If you cannot remember a trip’s departure time, please give an estimate and mark the box for estimates. If you cannot remember whether a trip happened, leave that part blank rather than filling in a trip you think probably happened.

One adult may complete the form for the household, checking with other members where possible. We ask how many people live in your household and their age bands, but not their names.

Your invitation has a code that lets us stop reminders when your form arrives. The team receiving completed forms can see this code. An address list links the codes to homes, so responses are not anonymous while we keep that list. We will delete the list after reminders finish. Reminders are scheduled to finish at the end of the following month.

Taking part is voluntary. You may skip any question. Returning an incomplete form will stop reminders just as returning a complete form will.

After the address list has been deleted, we cannot remove a response because we will no longer be able to link a household’s request to its form. We will publish results for groups of blocks, not individual households.

We hope you will help, including if your household’s whole travel story that day is that everyone stayed home.

This figure described the initial respondents, as the preliminary note stated. It did not establish the percentage among all invited households, although it was sometimes interpreted that way.

The telephone follow-up added information from 90 of the 240 initial nonrespondents. Interviewers stopped when they reached the budgeted total of 90 completed interviews. These households were not a simple random sample of the initial nonrespondents: inclusion depended on whether interviewers could reach them and whether they agreed to participate. Of the 90, 42 reported library use in the previous month, or approximately 46.7 percent.

Combining the two stages gives 294 reports of library use among 450 responding households, or approximately 65.3 percent. The decline from 70 to 65.3 percent shows how the descriptive result changed when the follow-up households joined the respondent pool. The follow-up respondents reported library use less often than the initial respondents. Although both stages used the same question and reference month, households were not randomly assigned to questionnaire or telephone modes. We therefore cannot separate differences between the people reached from any effect of how the question was administered.

The follow-up broadened the observed group, but it did not establish that nonresponse had been corrected. No weights or imputed responses were used, and 150 households still provided no response. We do not know whether those households resemble either responding group. Treating the combined percentage as an estimate for all 600 invitees would require assumptions that this study did not evaluate.

The report should retain the results from both stages and present 65.3 percent as the percentage among all responding households. This preserves the follow-up’s concrete contribution—additional responses that changed the observed result—while making clear that library use among all invited households remains unknown.

# What the Follow-Up Changes and What Remains Unknown

An early return rate can look like an answer to a question it has not answered. In our survey of library use, 600 households were invited and 360 returned the initial questionnaire. Of those 360, 252 reported using a library in the previous month, which is 70 percent of initial respondents. This figure appeared in the preliminary note, which described it as a finding about respondents. In later discussion it was sometimes treated as a description of all invited households, and that reading is not supported.

**What the follow-up added.** We approached the 240 initial nonrespondents by telephone. The follow-up budget covered 90 completed interviews, and interviewers worked through contact attempts until 90 were done. The 90 households are therefore not a simple random sample of the 240. Which households entered the group depended on whether interviewers could reach them and whether they agreed to take part. Forty-two of the 90 reported library use in the previous month, about 46.7 percent. The question and reference month were the same as in the questionnaire, but mode was not randomly assigned.

Combining the two stages gives 294 reports of library use among 450 responding households, about 65.3 percent. The shift from 70 to 65.3 percent is a change in the observed respondent pool. It shows that the initial respondents and the reached follow-up respondents differed in what they reported, and this is the concrete information the follow-up contributed.

**What the follow-up does not settle.** The combined figure does not tell us the prevalence among all 600 invitees, because 150 households still gave no response. It also cannot separate two explanations for the gap between 70 and 46.7 percent. One is a telephone-mode effect on how people answered. The other is a real difference between the people who answered by questionnaire and the people reached by phone. Without random assignment of mode, the two are entangled.

**Not an adjustment for nonresponse.** We considered describing the follow-up as an adjustment for nonresponse. In a descriptive sense it does broaden the observed group by including people absent from the first calculation. In the statistical sense, though, saying the remaining nonresponse has been corrected would require assumptions that we have not evaluated. No weights or imputed responses were used, and the combined figure should not be read as a corrected estimate.

**Recommendation for reporting.** The report should keep both stages visible rather than replacing the first percentage with a supposedly final population estimate:

| Stage | Households | Reported library use | Percent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial questionnaire | 360 | 252 | 70.0 |
| Telephone follow-up | 90 | 42 | about 46.7 |
| Combined respondents | 450 | 294 | about 65.3 |
| No response | 150 | unknown | unknown |

We recommend keeping completed interviews in the weekly dashboard while ending the practice of ranking interviewers by that number alone. The count tells us whether fieldwork is moving, but it does not tell us enough to compare people whose assigned routes differ.

Some routes contain apartment buildings with a staffed entrance. Others contain scattered homes that require long walks between attempts. Although assignments rotate each month, the dashboard ranks interviewers each week. Rotation may spread difficult routes over a longer period without making any particular week’s assignments comparable. We have not estimated how large that difference is.

The ranking also leaves out work that does not produce a completed interview. A careful refusal record or a return visit at the requested time may be necessary fieldwork even when no completed questionnaire results. Including those activities in the discussion would not mean treating every attempt as equally useful. Supervisors would still need to look at what happened and whether the agreed contact procedure was followed.

We do not propose replacing the ranking with a single weighted score. We have no tested weights, and a score could conceal the same judgment inside a formula. Instead, for the next four weeks, the dashboard should show completed interviews, attempts, and route assignments together, with supervisors adding a brief explanation when discussing unusual totals.

This arrangement will take more attention than reading a league table, and that cost is part of the recommendation. It may also reveal problems that the old ranking missed, but we cannot claim that it will improve response rates before trying it. At the end of four weeks, the steering group should ask whether the added context led to useful changes in supervisory decisions and whether the burden was manageable. The aim is to make the weekly discussion more informative while preserving a clear view of fieldwork progress.

\[
\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,
\qquad
\sigma^2=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2.
\]
Choose an unordered pair \(P\) uniformly from the \(\binom N2\) pairs, then choose \(J\) uniformly from the two indices in \(P\). Set
\[
Y=y_J,
\qquad
Z=\frac12\sum_{i\in P}y_i.
\]
All expectations and variances below refer to this sampling procedure; the population responses are fixed. We show that
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]

Each index \(i\) belongs to \(N-1\) pairs. Thus
\[
\Pr(J=i)=\frac{N-1}{\binom N2}\cdot\frac12=\frac1N.
\]
Consequently, \(Y\) is a uniformly sampled population response, so
\[
\mathbb E[Y]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2.
\]

Conditional on \(P=\{i,j\}\), the variable \(Y\) takes the values \(y_i\) and \(y_j\) with equal probabilities, while \(Z=(y_i+y_j)/2\) is fixed. Hence
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]=0.
\]
Averaging the first identity over the possible pairs gives
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[Y\mid P]\right]
=\mathbb E[Y]=\mu.
\]

To obtain the variance, write
\[
Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu).
\]
The cross term has expectation zero. Indeed, conditioning on \(P\) makes \(Z-\mu\) a fixed multiplier, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)\mid P]\right]\\
&=\mathbb E\!\left[(Z-\mu)\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\right]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Squaring the decomposition and taking expectations therefore yields
\[
\sigma^2
=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z).
\]
This step uses the zero conditional mean of \(Y-Z\), not independence of \(Y\) and \(Z\).

For a given pair \(P=\{i,j\}\), the two possible values of \(Y-Z\) are \((y_i-y_j)/2\) and its negative. Therefore,
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
\]
Averaging over the uniformly chosen pairs gives
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
=\frac{1}{4\binom N2}\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2.
\]
Expanding the squared differences establishes the finite-population identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=N\sum_i y_i^2-\left(\sum_i y_i\right)^2\\
&=N\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2
=N^2\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]=\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)},
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(Z)
=\sigma^2-\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.}

# Appendix: Mean and variance of the pair-mean estimator

**Setup.** Let N ≥ 2 and let y₁, …, y_N be fixed real numbers. Define

μ = N⁻¹ Σᵢ yᵢ and σ² = N⁻¹ Σᵢ (yᵢ − μ)².

Draw an unordered pair P uniformly from the C(N,2) pairs of indices. Then draw J uniformly from the two indices in P. Set

Y = y_J and Z = ½ Σ_{i∈P} yᵢ.

**Claim.** E[Z] = μ and Var(Z) = (N−2)σ² / (2(N−1)).

All randomness comes from the sampling design (P and J). The responses yᵢ are fixed constants, so the expectations and variances describe repeated sampling from this population.

The proof compares Y, a single draw, with Z, the mean of the pair containing it. Y and Z are dependent, since Z is determined by P and Y is drawn from within P. The argument never needs them to be independent, only a conditional-mean identity.

## Step 1: Y is a uniform draw from the population

Each index i lies in exactly N−1 of the C(N,2) pairs, so P(i ∈ P) = (N−1)/C(N,2) = 2/N. Given i ∈ P, J = i with probability 1/2. Hence

P(J = i) = (2/N)(1/2) = 1/N for every i.

So Y is a simple random draw from {y₁, …, y_N}, and

E[Y] = μ, Var(Y) = E[(Y−μ)²] = σ².

## Step 2: Conditional on the pair

Fix P = {i, j}. Given P, Y equals yᵢ or yⱼ with probability ½ each. Therefore

E[Y | P] = (yᵢ + yⱼ)/2 = Z,

and, since Y − Z = ±(yᵢ − yⱼ)/2,

E[(Y−Z)² | P = {i,j}] = (yᵢ − yⱼ)² / 4.

## Step 3: The mean of Z

By the first identity in Step 2 and the tower property,

E[Z] = E[E[Y | P]] = E[Y] = μ.

## Step 4: Decomposing σ²

Write Y − μ = (Y − Z) + (Z − μ) and square:

E[(Y−μ)²] = E[(Y−Z)²] + 2E[(Y−Z)(Z−μ)] + E[(Z−μ)²].

The cross term vanishes. Z − μ is a function of P, so it can be taken outside the conditional expectation:

E[(Y−Z)(Z−μ)] = E[(Z−μ) · E[Y−Z | P]] = E[(Z−μ) · 0] = 0.

This uses only E[Y − Z | P] = 0 from Step 2, not independence of Y and Z. Since E[Z] = μ, the last term is Var(Z). With Step 1, this gives

σ² = E[(Y−Z)²] + Var(Z). (1)

## Step 5: Computing E[(Y−Z)²]

Averaging the second identity in Step 2 over the C(N,2) equally likely pairs gives

E[(Y−Z)²] = (1 / (4·C(N,2))) Σ_{i<j} (yᵢ − yⱼ)².

For the sum, note that Σ_{i<j} = ½ Σᵢ Σⱼ, so

Σ_{i<j} (yᵢ − yⱼ)² = ½ Σᵢ Σⱼ (yᵢ² − 2yᵢyⱼ + yⱼ²)
 = N Σᵢ yᵢ² − (Σᵢ yᵢ)²
 = N [Σᵢ yᵢ² − Nμ²]
 = N Σᵢ (yᵢ − μ)²
 = N² σ².

Since 4·C(N,2) = 2N(N−1),

E[(Y−Z)²] = N²σ² / (2N(N−1)) = Nσ² / (2(N−1)). (2)

## Step 6: Conclusion

Substituting (2) into (1):

Var(Z) = σ² − Nσ² / (2(N−1)) = σ² · (2(N−1) − N) / (2(N−1)) = (N−2)σ² / (2(N−1)). ∎

**Step 2: The marginal law of $Y$.** Each index $i$ belongs to exactly $N-1$ of the pairs, so
$$
\mathbb P(J=i)=\frac{N-1}{\binom N2}\cdot\frac12=\frac{N-1}{N(N-1)/2}\cdot\frac12=\frac1N .
$$
Thus $J$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,N\}$, and therefore
$$
\mathbb E[Y]=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2 .
$$
Taking expectations in $\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z$ gives $\mathbb E[Z]=\mathbb E[Y]=\mu$.

**Step 3: Decomposition of $\sigma^2$.** Write $Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu)$ and expand the square:
$$
\sigma^2=\mathbb E[(Y-\mu)^2]
=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+2\,\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]+\mathbb E[(Z-\mu)^2].
$$
The last term is $\operatorname{Var}(Z)$ because $\mathbb E[Z]=\mu$. For the cross term, $Z$ is a function of $P$, so $Z-\mu$ can be taken outside the conditional expectation given $P$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\Big[\mathbb E\big[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)\mid P\big]\Big]\\
&=\mathbb E\Big[(Z-\mu)\,\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\Big]\\
&=0,
\end{aligned}
$$
where the last equality uses $\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z$ from Step 1. This argument uses only that $Z$ is determined by $P$. It does not assume that $Y$ and $Z$ are independent, and they are not. We conclude
$$
\sigma^2=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z). \tag{1}
$$

**Step 4: The term $\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]$.** Since $P$ is uniform over the $\binom N2$ pairs, Step 1 gives
$$
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
=\frac{1}{\binom N2}\sum_{i<j}\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
$$
To evaluate the sum, note that the ordered double sum counts each unordered pair twice and has zero diagonal terms:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N (y_i-y_j)^2\\
&=\frac12\Big(2N\sum_i y_i^2-2\Big(\sum_i y_i\Big)^2\Big)\\
&=N\sum_i y_i^2-\Big(\sum_i y_i\Big)^2\\
&=N\sum_i (y_i-\mu)^2\\
&=N^2\sigma^2 .
\end{aligned}
$$
The fourth line uses $\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2=\sum_i y_i^2-N\mu^2=\sum_i y_i^2-\frac1N\big(\sum_i y_i\big)^2$. Since $4\binom N2=2N(N-1)$,
$$
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]=\frac{N^2\sigma^2}{2N(N-1)}=\frac{N}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2 .
$$

**Step 5: Conclusion.** Substituting into (1) and subtracting,
$$
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\sigma^2-\frac{N}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2
=\frac{2(N-1)-N}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2 .
$$

**Edge cases.** For $N=2$ the only pair is the whole population, so $Z=\mu$ is constant, which agrees with the formula's value $0$. If all responses are equal, then $\sigma^2=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=0$ for every $N$. The argument never divides by $\sigma^2$, so these cases need no separate treatment. $\qquad\blacksquare$

Let \(K=\ker A\), and let \(P\) be the orthogonal projection onto \(K^\perp\). Assume
\[
\|Av\|_2\ge \gamma\|v\|_2\qquad(v\in K^\perp),
\]
where \(\gamma>0\). Suppose \(y=Ax+e\) with \(\|e\|_2\le\varepsilon\), and let \(\hat x\) be any least-squares minimizer. We show that
\[
\|P(\hat x-x)\|_2\le \frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}.
\]

Put \(h=\hat x-x\). The normal equations give
\[
A^\top(A\hat x-y)=A^\top(Ah-e)=0.
\]
Multiplying by \(h^\top\) and applying Cauchy–Schwarz yields
\[
\|Ah\|_2^2=\langle Ah,e\rangle
\le \|Ah\|_2\|e\|_2
\le \varepsilon\|Ah\|_2.
\]
If \(Ah\ne0\), division gives \(\|Ah\|_2\le\varepsilon\); the same conclusion holds when \(Ah=0\).

Now decompose \(h=Ph+(I-P)h\). Since \((I-P)h\in K\), we have \(A(I-P)h=0\), so \(Ah=A(Ph)\). Because \(Ph\in K^\perp\), the assumed lower bound applies to \(Ph\), giving
\[
\gamma\|Ph\|_2\le \|A(Ph)\|_2=\|Ah\|_2\le\varepsilon.
\]
Dividing by \(\gamma\) proves the claim.

When \(\varepsilon=0\), this gives \(P\hat x=Px\), so the observable component is recovered exactly. It does not imply uniqueness of \(\hat x\): adding any vector in \(K\) preserves the least-squares objective. If \(K^\perp=\{0\}\), then \(P=0\) and the claimed bound holds trivially. No bound on the error component in \(K\) is asserted. \(\square\)

**Claim.** Under the stated hypotheses, every least-squares minimizer x̂ satisfies ‖P(x̂ − x)‖₂ ≤ ε/γ.

**Setup.** Let K = {v ∈ ℝᵈ : Av = 0}, and let P be the orthogonal projection onto K^⊥. Then I − P is the orthogonal projection onto K. Let x̂ minimize ‖Az − y‖₂ over z ∈ ℝᵈ. A minimizer exists because the range of A is a closed subspace of ℝʳ, so y has a nearest point Az₀ in it. Put h = x̂ − x.

**Step 1: the residual equation.** A minimizer of ‖Az − y‖₂² satisfies the normal equations Aᵀ(Ax̂ − y) = 0. Since y = Ax + e,

Ax̂ − y = A(x̂ − x) − e = Ah − e,

so Aᵀ(Ah − e) = 0.

**Step 2: the image of the error is small.** Multiply on the left by hᵀ:

0 = hᵀAᵀ(Ah − e) = ⟨Ah, Ah − e⟩,

so ‖Ah‖₂² = ⟨Ah, e⟩. By Cauchy–Schwarz and ‖e‖₂ ≤ ε,

‖Ah‖₂² ≤ ‖Ah‖₂ ‖e‖₂ ≤ ‖Ah‖₂ ε.

If Ah ≠ 0, dividing by ‖Ah‖₂ gives ‖Ah‖₂ ≤ ε. If Ah = 0, then ‖Ah‖₂ = 0 ≤ ε trivially. In either case,

‖Ah‖₂ ≤ ε.  (1)

**Step 3: the repair, passing to the observable component.** The draft applied the lower bound to h itself, but h need not lie in K^⊥. Instead, decompose

h = Ph + (I − P)h, with Ph ∈ K^⊥ and (I − P)h ∈ K.

Because (I − P)h ∈ K, we have A(I − P)h = 0, and therefore

Ah = APh + A(I − P)h = APh.  (2)

Now Ph ∈ K^⊥, so the hypothesis ‖Av‖₂ ≥ γ‖v‖₂ for v ∈ K^⊥ applies to v = Ph. Combining it with (2) and (1):

γ‖Ph‖₂ ≤ ‖APh‖₂ = ‖Ah‖₂ ≤ ε.

Since γ > 0, dividing gives

- **ε = 0.** Then ‖Ah‖₂ = 0, so Ph = 0 and the component of x in K^⊥ is recovered exactly: Px̂ = Px. This does not make x̂ unique. Any x̂ + k with k ∈ K is also a least-squares minimizer, because Ak = 0 leaves the residual unchanged.
- **K^⊥ = {0}.** Then A = 0 and P = 0, so the left side is 0 and the bound holds trivially. The lower-bound hypothesis is vacuous, and the argument above goes through unchanged.

**Setup.** Let K = {v ∈ ℝ^d : Av = 0} and let P be the orthogonal projection onto K^⊥. Suppose y = Ax + e with ‖e‖₂ ≤ ε and ε ≥ 0, and suppose that for some γ > 0

$$
\|Av\|_2 \ge \gamma \|v\|_2 \qquad \text{for every } v \in K^\perp .
$$

Let x̂ be any minimizer of ‖Az − y‖₂ over z ∈ ℝ^d. A minimizer exists because the range of A is a subspace of ℝ^r, which is closed, so it contains a point nearest to y. We claim

$$
\|P(\hat x - x)\|_2 \le \frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}.
$$

This bounds only the component of the error in K^⊥. The matrix A does not see the component in K, and nothing here bounds it.

**Step 1: a bound on Ah.** Put h = x̂ − x. Since x̂ minimizes the quadratic ‖Az − y‖₂², its gradient vanishes there, which gives the normal equations Aᵀ(Ax̂ − y) = 0. Because y = Ax + e,

$$
A\hat x - y = A(\hat x - x) - e = Ah - e,
$$

so

$$
A^\top (Ah - e) = 0 .
$$

Multiplying on the left by hᵀ and using Cauchy–Schwarz,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|Ah\|_2^2 &= \langle Ah, e\rangle \\
&\le \|Ah\|_2 \,\|e\|_2 \\
&\le \|Ah\|_2\, \varepsilon .
\end{aligned}
$$

If Ah ≠ 0, dividing by ‖Ah‖₂ gives ‖Ah‖₂ ≤ ε. If Ah = 0, the same inequality holds trivially. In both cases

$$
\|Ah\|_2 \le \varepsilon. \tag{1}
$$

**Step 2: passing to the component in K^⊥.** The lower bound on A applies only to vectors in K^⊥, and h need not lie there. So we split h as

$$
h = Ph + (I-P)h .
$$

Here (I − P)h is the orthogonal projection of h onto K, hence A(I − P)h = 0. Therefore

$$
Ah = A Ph + A(I-P)h = A Ph. \tag{2}
$$

Since Ph ∈ K^⊥, the assumed lower bound applies to it. Combining it with (2) and (1),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma \|Ph\|_2 &\le \|A Ph\|_2 \\
&= \|Ah\|_2 \\
&\le \varepsilon .
\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by γ > 0 gives

$$
\|P(\hat x - x)\|_2 = \|Ph\|_2 \le \frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma},
$$

which is the claim. ∎

**Special cases.**

- If ε = 0, the bound gives P(x̂ − x) = 0, so the component of x̂ in K^⊥ equals that of x. The minimizer need not be unique, because x̂ + k is also a minimizer for every k ∈ K.
- If K^⊥ = {0}, then P = 0 and the claim is trivial. The hypothesis on γ holds vacuously.

At the start of each shift, place the probe in the reference fixture and record its reading. The acceptance band is 48 to 52 units, including both endpoints. This check compares the probe with a stable reference block. It does not measure the temperature of material currently on the line, and a reading inside the band does not by itself authorize a production restart.

During the six-week trial, if the first reference-block reading is outside the acceptance band, let the probe rest in the fixture for ten minutes, then repeat the reading once. The rest period applies only before the repeat; the start-of-shift check and acceptance band are unchanged. Record both readings in the shift log before making any required call. If the repeat is also outside the band, call the shift lead, who will decide whether a further check is needed. If the repeat is within the band, no call is required by this rule. Do not change the probe's offset in response to this check. The trial concerns the escalation process, not permission for operators to recalibrate the instrument.

For the weekly trend chart, use the first reading from each shift, including first readings outside the acceptance band. Keep any repeat readings in the log, but do not substitute them into the chart. This keeps the plotted sequence tied to the same point in the checking process, even when the escalation procedure calls for more than one observation.

The maintenance team will review the log and the chart at the end of the trial. A charted outlier is a reason to examine the record, not a diagnosis of a failed probe. Please include notes about a loose fixture or an interrupted check where relevant. Those notes help explain what happened, but they do not replace the numerical readings.
